newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Germany, Italy bunch in EMU race-OECD.
newsitem.headline: France, Germany, Italy bunch in EMU race-OECD.

text.p: Italy, France and Germany are likely to be neck-and-neck in their efforts to cut budget deficits and qualify for European monetary union this year, according to forecasts published by the OECD on Thursday.

It forecast all three showing total public deficits of 3.2 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, just shy of a strict reading of the Maastricht treaty which calls for deficits to be reduced to 3.0 percent of GDP.
But the OECD's chief economist said the decision due in April/May 1998 on which countries qualify for economic and monetary union in 1999 should not be based on decimal points.

"The decision will be political. From an economic point of view, it would seem anomalous to exclude a few countries on the basis of a few decimal points," OECD chief economist Stephen Potter told a news conference.
The forecasts, which some economists said might already be outdated, had little impact on financial markets.
But economists said they pointed to broad EMU membership, rather than the narrow one sought by Bonn which is trying to cut its deficit to 3.0 percent.
"(The forecast) is not bad enough to provoke thoughts of delay (in EMU)," Nomura economist Sonja Gibbs said. "On the face of it, if it has any impact at all, it is definitely broad EMU friendly."

The Organisation for Economic and Co-operation and Development also forecast in its half-year economic outlook that Germany and France would cut their deficits further in 1998, to 2.7 and 3.0 percent of GDP respectively. But Italy's deficit/GDP ratio was seen as rising to 3.8 percent.
Officials have insisted deficit cuts must be sustainable, in what some see as a warning to Italy that it may be left out of EMU if it cannot keep up its 1997 performance.
The OECD's 1998 forecast for Italy did not take account of a three-year plan promised by Rome to cut its debt and deficit, nor of a likely fall in Italian interest rates if it does join EMU in 1999.
"I think (the forecasts) are quite bullish for Italy," UBS economist Darren Williams said.
Spain and Portugal, whose chances of joining EMU in 1999 are often seen as linked to Italy's prospects, were given top EMU marks by the OECD.
It saw Spain's deficit/GDP ratio at 3.0 percent in 1997 and 2.6 percent in 1998, and Portugal's at 2.9 percent in 1997 and 2.8 percent in 1998.
Spain's determination to join EMU in 1999 has been a key factor in convincing Italy that it must not be left behind.

Economists said in any case the deficit/GDP ratios probably mattered less than political developments in Europe, particularly in France where the new Socialist-led government has been fighting to end austerity in the EU.

France has said it wants Italy and Spain to join EMU at the start, that there should be a flexible interpretion of the Maastricht treaty and that it will not impose new austerity just to cut the deficit/GDP ratio to exactly 3.0 percent.
"The ball is still in France's court," Gibbs said.
